Course.title: AS.110.106 Calculus I (Biology and Social Sciences)
Course.assumed_background: High-school algebra, coordinate geometry, and basic trigonometry; no prior calculus required.

Module.title: Review Basic Properties of Functions
Module.goal: Review the function families, exponential models, and sequences that the rest of the course builds on.

Module.title: Limits and Continuity
Module.goal: Develop the limit concept, informally and formally, and use it to define and analyze continuity.

Module.title: Derivatives
Module.goal: Define the derivative as a limit and master the rules for differentiating the standard function families.

Module.title: Applications of Differentiation
Module.goal: Use derivatives to analyze function shape, find extrema, solve optimization problems, and evaluate indeterminate limits.

Module.title: Integration
Module.goal: Introduce antiderivatives and the definite integral, and connect them through the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

Module.title: Applications of the Integral
Module.goal: Extend integration with substitution, integration by parts, and partial fractions so a wider range of integrals can be evaluated.

Concept.name: Functions, graphs, and transformations
Concept.summary: A function assigns each input in its domain exactly one output. Domain, range, graphs, composition, inverses, and shifts/stretches are the basic toolkit for everything that follows.
key_definitions: Function: a rule assigning exactly one output to each input in the domain
Inverse function: f^-1 satisfies f^-1(f(x)) = x; it exists when f is one-to-one

difficulty_notes.misconception: Treating f(g(x)) as g(f(x)) or as the product f(x)g(x).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Evaluate both compositions numerically at one point, then in a biological chain (dose → concentration → response) where the order obviously matters.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Believing f(x-2) shifts the graph to the left.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Tabulate a few points of f(x) and f(x-2) and plot them to see the shift is to the right.

Concept.name: Polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions
Concept.summary: The standard function families, their graphs, and the algebraic laws (exponent, logarithm, trig identities) used to simplify expressions and solve equations.
key_definitions: Logarithm: log_b(x) = y if and only if b^y = x
Rational function: a ratio of two polynomials

difficulty_notes.misconception: Believing ln(a + b) = ln(a) + ln(b).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Test with a = b = 1, then restate the law: logs turn products into sums, not sums into sums.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Mixing degrees and radians when evaluating trig functions.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Fix radians as the default from the start and convert once with π rad = 180°.

Concept.name: Exponential growth and decay
Concept.summary: Quantities whose rate of change is proportional to their size follow N(t) = N0·e^(rt); r > 0 gives growth and r < 0 gives decay. Doubling times and half-lives summarize the rate.
key_definitions: Half-life: time for a quantity to fall to half its value
Growth rate r versus growth factor b per time step

difficulty_notes.misconception: Confusing the continuous rate r with the per-step growth factor b (b = e^r, not 1 + r in general).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Write the same data in both forms and convert between them explicitly.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Treating exponential decay as linear decay over several half-lives.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Tabulate the amount remaining after each half-life to show repeated halving, not repeated subtraction.

Concept.name: Sequences and their limits
Concept.summary: A sequence is a function on the positive integers. Sequences can be given explicitly or recursively (difference equations), and their long-run behavior is described by limits and equilibria.
key_definitions: Limit of a sequence: a_n → L as n → ∞
Equilibrium (fixed point) a* satisfying a* = f(a*)

difficulty_notes.misconception: Assuming a sequence converges because successive terms get closer together (e.g. a_n = sqrt(n)).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Check whether the terms approach a fixed number; compare sqrt(n) with 1/n numerically.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Confusing the equilibrium a* with the initial value or the constant term of the recursion.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Substitute a_(n+1) = a_n = a* and solve the resulting equation explicitly.

Concept.name: Limits (informal and one-sided)
Concept.summary: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x approaches a, regardless of the value at a. The limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree; algebra resolves 0/0 forms.
key_definitions: One-sided limits from the left and right
Limit laws for sums, products, and quotients
0/0 form: requires algebraic simplification before evaluating

difficulty_notes.misconception: Believing the limit at a must equal f(a), or that 0/0 means the limit does not exist.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use removable-hole examples like (x^2-1)/(x-1), then factor and cancel to show the limit exists.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Concluding a limit exists after checking only one side.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Always compute left and right limits separately for piecewise and absolute-value functions.

Concept.name: Formal (epsilon-delta) definition of a limit
Concept.summary: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L if for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that 0 < |x - a| < δ implies |f(x) - L| < ε. This makes 'arbitrarily close' precise and supports rigorous proofs of limits.
key_definitions: Epsilon-delta definition of lim_{x→a} f(x) = L
δ as a function of ε

difficulty_notes.misconception: Picking δ first, or believing one δ works for every ε; the quantifier order is reversed.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Present it as a game: the challenger names ε, then you must produce δ; do scratch work backward from |f(x) - L| < ε.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Thinking that checking a few specific values of ε proves the limit.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Emphasize that the proof must work for an arbitrary ε, by writing δ as a formula in ε.

Concept.name: Continuity and types of discontinuity
Concept.summary: f is continuous at a if f(a) is defined, lim_{x→a} f(x) exists, and the two are equal. Failures are classified as removable, jump, or infinite discontinuities.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Judging continuity only by whether the graph can be drawn without lifting the pen, which mishandles functions like 1/x that are continuous on their domain.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Check the three conditions explicitly and distinguish 'continuous on its domain' from 'continuous everywhere'.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Assuming a limit that exists implies continuity.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use the removable-hole example where the limit exists but f(a) is missing or misplaced.

Concept.name: Limits at infinity and horizontal asymptotes
Concept.summary: lim_{x→∞} f(x) = L means f(x) stays within any ε of L once x is large enough. Comparing dominant terms evaluates rational functions, and the limit describes the long-run behavior of biological models.
key_definitions: Limit at infinity (formal): for each ε > 0 there is M such that x > M implies |f(x) - L| < ε

difficulty_notes.misconception: Treating ∞ as a number (e.g. ∞/∞ = 1 or ∞ - ∞ = 0).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Divide numerator and denominator by the highest power of x and verify numerically with large x.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Assuming a function that keeps growing has no horizontal asymptote, or that one that levels off must reach its limit.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Compare C(t) = 20t/(t+4) with t and show it increases yet stays below 20.

Concept.name: Trigonometric limits and the Sandwich Theorem
Concept.summary: If g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) near a and g and h both tend to L, then f tends to L. This yields lim sin(x)/x = 1 and lim (1 - cos x)/x = 0 as x → 0, which underpin trig derivatives.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Claiming sin(x)/x → 0 or is undefined at 0 because of the 0/0 form, or using degrees.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Tabulate sin(x)/x for small radian values and sketch the unit-circle area argument.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Forgetting to rescale: treating lim sin(5x)/x as 1.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Multiply and divide by 5 so the argument of sin matches the denominator.

Concept.name: Properties of continuous functions and the Intermediate Value Theorem
Concept.summary: Sums, products, quotients (with nonzero denominator), and compositions of continuous functions are continuous. The Intermediate Value Theorem says a continuous f on [a, b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b).

difficulty_notes.misconception: Applying the IVT without checking continuity, or treating the converse as true (no sign change means no root).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use f(x) = 1/x on [-1, 1] and f(x) = x^2 on [-1, 1] as counterexamples.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Believing the IVT identifies a unique root.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Show a cubic that crosses zero three times while the endpoint signs differ.

Concept.name: Formal definition of the derivative
Concept.summary: f'(a) = lim_{h→0} (f(a+h) - f(a))/h is the slope of the tangent line and the instantaneous rate of change. Differentiability implies continuity, but not conversely.
key_definitions: Derivative f'(a) as a limit of difference quotients
Tangent line y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)

difficulty_notes.misconception: Confusing the average rate of change over [a, a+h] with the instantaneous rate.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Compute secant slopes for shrinking h and watch them converge to the tangent slope.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Believing continuous functions are always differentiable.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Examine |x| at 0, where the left and right difference quotients disagree.

Concept.name: Basic rules of differentiation
Concept.summary: The derivative of a constant is 0, constants factor out, and the derivative of a sum or difference is the sum or difference of derivatives (linearity). Linear functions have constant derivative equal to their slope.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Treating a constant like a variable, e.g. d/dx of π = 1 or d/dx 5 = 5.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Graph a horizontal line and read its slope as 0; the difference quotient is identically 0.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Interpreting P'(t) without units or meaning.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Always state the units of the derivative (units of P per unit of t) in word problems.

Concept.name: Power rule
Concept.summary: d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1) for any real exponent n, including negative and fractional ones. Combined with linearity, it differentiates polynomials, roots, and reciprocals.
key_definitions: Power rule: d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1)
Rewriting roots and reciprocals as powers

difficulty_notes.misconception: Applying the power rule to exponentials such as 2^x, writing x·2^(x-1).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Contrast x^2 (variable base) with 2^x (variable exponent) and defer 2^x to the exponential rule.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Failing to rewrite sqrt(x) or 1/x^2 as powers before differentiating.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Make the rewrite step explicit in every worked example.

Concept.name: Product and quotient rules
Concept.summary: (fg)' = f'g + fg' and (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g^2. These handle products and ratios of differentiable functions where term-by-term differentiation fails.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Writing (fg)' = f'g'.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Test with f = g = x: (x^2)' = 2x, not 1.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Reversing the order of the numerator in the quotient rule, producing a sign error.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use the mnemonic 'low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared' and check the sign on a simple example.

Concept.name: The chain rule
Concept.summary: (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x))·g'(x): differentiate the outer function at the inner function, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function. It is the key rule for composite functions.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Forgetting to multiply by the derivative of the inner function.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Label inner and outer functions in writing and differentiate each explicitly.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Evaluating f' at x instead of at g(x).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Write the outer derivative with a placeholder first, e.g. 5(□)^4, then fill in the inner function.

Concept.name: Implicit functions and implicit differentiation
Concept.summary: When y is defined implicitly by an equation in x and y, differentiate both sides with respect to x, treat y as y(x) using the chain rule, and solve for dy/dx.
key_definitions: dy/dx as a function of both x and y

difficulty_notes.misconception: Differentiating y-terms without the factor dy/dx (e.g. d/dx y^2 = 2y).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Rewrite y as y(x) so the chain rule is visible: d/dx [y(x)]^2 = 2y y'.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Forgetting the product rule on mixed terms like xy, or forgetting to substitute the point after solving for dy/dx.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use a fixed checklist: differentiate, collect y' terms, factor, solve, substitute.

Concept.name: Higher derivatives
Concept.summary: The second derivative f'' is the derivative of f' and measures how the slope changes (acceleration, concavity). Higher derivatives f^(n) continue the process.
key_definitions: Acceleration as the second derivative of position

difficulty_notes.misconception: Confusing f''(x) with (f'(x))^2 or stopping after the first derivative.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Emphasize notation: f'' means differentiate twice; compute both side by side for a simple polynomial.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Not interpreting the units or sign of the second derivative.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Tie f'' to acceleration in a motion example and to the curvature of a graph.

Concept.name: Derivatives of trigonometric functions
Concept.summary: d/dx sin x = cos x, d/dx cos x = -sin x, and d/dx tan x = sec^2 x, all with x in radians. These follow from the limit of sin(x)/x and combine with the chain rule.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Dropping the minus sign in the derivative of cosine.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Check against the graph: cos is decreasing just after x = 0, so its slope must be negative.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Omitting the chain-rule factor for sin(kx), e.g. d/dx sin(3x) = cos(3x).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Label inner function kx and multiply by k.

Concept.name: Derivatives of exponential and logarithmic functions
Concept.summary: d/dx e^x = e^x, d/dx a^x = a^x ln(a), and d/dx ln x = 1/x. With the chain rule, d/dx e^(g(x)) = g'(x) e^(g(x)), which shows exponential growth has rate proportional to size.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Applying the power rule to e^x, writing x·e^(x-1).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Contrast variable base with variable exponent; e^x is its own derivative.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Forgetting the factor ln(a) when differentiating a^x.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Rewrite a^x as e^(x ln a) and apply the chain rule.

Concept.name: Derivatives of inverse functions
Concept.summary: If g = f^-1, then g'(y) = 1/f'(g(y)). This formula explains the derivative of ln x and gives derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Evaluating f' at y instead of at the point f^-1(y), or reading f^-1 as 1/f.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Reflect points over y = x to track which variable is which, and find f^-1(y) first.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Not seeing that (ln x)' = 1/x follows from (e^x)' = e^x.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Derive it with the inverse formula in class before memorizing.

Concept.name: Linear approximation
Concept.summary: Near x = a, f(x) ≈ L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a). Linearization estimates function values and changes, and concavity tells whether the estimate is high or low.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Using the linearization far from a or omitting the f(a) term.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Plot f and L together to show where they separate; write L as a tangent line through (a, f(a)).

difficulty_notes.misconception: Not knowing whether the tangent line over- or underestimates.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use concavity: concave down means the tangent lies above the curve (overestimate).

Concept.name: Extreme Value Theorem and Mean Value Theorem
Concept.summary: A continuous function on a closed interval attains an absolute maximum and minimum. If it is also differentiable on the open interval, the Mean Value Theorem gives a point where the instantaneous rate equals the average rate. Interior extrema occur at critical points.
key_definitions: Critical point: f'(c) = 0 or f'(c) undefined
Mean Value Theorem: f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a)

difficulty_notes.misconception: Applying the EVT on an open interval or to a discontinuous function.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Show f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1] has no maximum to make the hypotheses necessary.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Believing f'(c) = 0 guarantees an extremum at c.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Examine f(x) = x^3 at c = 0, where the derivative vanishes but f is increasing.

Concept.name: Monotonicity and concavity
Concept.summary: The sign of f' tells where f increases or decreases, and the sign of f'' tells where its graph is concave up or down. Sign charts organize this information to sketch a graph.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Confusing 'increasing' with 'concave up'.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Sketch all four combinations of the signs of f' and f'' and label biological examples, such as saturating growth being increasing and concave down.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Reading the sign of f' or f'' from a single test point or without testing each interval.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use a sign chart with one test point in every interval between critical points.

Concept.name: Extrema and inflection points
Concept.summary: Local extrema are located at critical points and classified by the first-derivative test or the second-derivative test. Inflection points occur where concavity changes, which requires a sign change of f'' and not just f'' = 0.
key_definitions: Inflection point: a point where concavity changes

difficulty_notes.misconception: Assuming f''(c) = 0 implies an inflection point (e.g. x^4 at 0).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Always verify a sign change in f'' on either side of c.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Ignoring endpoints and points where f' is undefined when seeking global extrema.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use a checklist: critical points, endpoints, points of non-differentiability.

Concept.name: Optimization
Concept.summary: Optimization problems are translated into maximizing or minimizing a function of one variable on a domain: define variables, write the objective, use the constraint to eliminate a variable, find critical points, check endpoints, and justify the result.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Skipping the constraint so the objective still has two variables, or ignoring the domain and endpoints.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use a checklist: diagram, variables, objective, constraint, domain, solve, verify, answer in context.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Reporting x instead of the quantity the problem asks for.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Require a final sentence that restates the answer with units.

Concept.name: L'Hopital's rule
Concept.summary: If lim f/g is of the form 0/0 or ∞/∞, then lim f/g = lim f'/g' whenever the latter limit exists. Other indeterminate forms (0·∞, ∞ - ∞) are first rewritten as quotients.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Differentiating the quotient with the quotient rule instead of differentiating numerator and denominator separately.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: State the rule as lim f'/g' and require writing f' and g' on separate lines.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Applying the rule when the limit is not indeterminate.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Make 'check the form first' an explicit first step, with a counterexample such as lim (x+1)/x as x → 0+.

Concept.name: Antiderivatives and indefinite integrals
Concept.summary: F is an antiderivative of f if F' = f. All antiderivatives differ by a constant, so the indefinite integral is written F(x) + C. Initial conditions determine C.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Forgetting +C, or applying the power formula at n = -1 (which gives ln|x|, not x^0/0).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Require differentiating the answer as a check, and treat 1/x as its own table entry.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Forgetting the 1/k factor for e^(kx) or cos(kx).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Differentiate the proposed antiderivative and see what factor appears.

Concept.name: The definite integral
Concept.summary: ∫_a^b f(x) dx is the limit of Riemann sums Σ f(x_i*) Δx and measures net signed area. It obeys linearity, additivity over intervals, and sign change when limits are reversed.
key_definitions: Definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums

difficulty_notes.misconception: Counting area below the axis as positive in a net-area integral, or confusing the definite integral (a number) with the indefinite integral (a family of functions).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Sketch the sign of f on each subinterval; show ∫ of sin over a full period is 0.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Forgetting the factor Δx in a Riemann sum.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Interpret each term f(x_i)·Δx as the area of a rectangle.

Concept.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
Concept.summary: Part 1: d/dx ∫_a^x f(t) dt = f(x). Part 2: ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a) for any antiderivative F. Together they link differentiation and integration.
key_definitions: FTC Part 1 (derivative of an accumulation function)

difficulty_notes.misconception: Forgetting the chain-rule factor g'(x) when the upper limit is g(x), or reversing F(b) - F(a).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Treat the upper limit as an inner function and write the evaluation with brackets and explicit order.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Believing the definite integral needs +C.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Show that C cancels in F(b) - F(a).

Concept.name: Applications of integration
Concept.summary: Definite integrals compute area between curves (top minus bottom), net change from a rate (total drug delivered), and average value (1/(b - a))∫ f.
key_definitions: Average value of a function (1/(b - a)) ∫_a^b f(x) dx

difficulty_notes.misconception: Subtracting in the wrong order, or not splitting the integral where the curves cross.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Sketch the curves first and label which is on top over each subinterval.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Computing the average value as the average of the endpoint values.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Compare against a nonlinear example, e.g. f(x) = x^2 on [0, 2].

Concept.name: The substitution rule
Concept.summary: ∫ f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du with u = g(x). It reverses the chain rule; for definite integrals the limits are converted to u-values.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Leaving some x's in the integral after substituting, or not converting the limits to u-values.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Write u, du, and new limits in a column before integrating, and differentiate the result to check.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Dropping a constant factor from du (e.g. treating 2x dx as x dx).
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Solve for dx or x dx explicitly: x dx = du/2.

Concept.name: Integration by parts
Concept.summary: ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du reverses the product rule. Choose u to simplify when differentiated (LIATE heuristic); it can be repeated and applied to definite integrals.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Choosing u and dv so the new integral is harder than the original.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Use LIATE and test both choices on a simple case like ∫ x e^x dx.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Sign errors or forgetting to integrate dv to get v.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Tabulate u, du, dv, v in a 2x2 grid before substituting.

Concept.name: Rational functions and partial fractions
Concept.summary: A proper rational function P/Q is decomposed into simpler fractions according to the factors of Q so each piece integrates to a logarithm or similar. Improper fractions are first divided.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Decomposing an improper fraction directly without long division.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Compare degrees of numerator and denominator as the very first step.

difficulty_notes.misconception: Writing the wrong form for repeated or irreducible factors, or mixing up which constant belongs to which factor.
difficulty_notes.mitigation: Solve for constants by substituting the roots of each factor, then check by recombining.

LearningObjective.text: Evaluate, compose, and invert functions, and sketch the effect of shifts and stretches on a graph.
Apply exponent, logarithm, and trigonometric laws to simplify expressions and solve equations.
Model growth and decay with exponential functions and compute doubling times and half-lives.
Compute limits of explicit and recursively defined sequences and find and interpret equilibria.
Evaluate limits algebraically, including one-sided limits and 0/0 forms, and decide when a limit does not exist.
State the epsilon-delta definition of a limit and prove simple linear limits with it.
Test continuity at a point using the three conditions and classify discontinuities.
Compute limits at infinity and interpret them as long-run behavior or horizontal asymptotes.
Apply the Sandwich Theorem and standard trigonometric limits to evaluate limits.
Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to justify the existence of solutions and justify continuity of composite functions.
Compute derivatives from the limit definition and interpret them as instantaneous rates of change and tangent slopes.
Differentiate constants, constant multiples, and sums, and interpret the result in context.
Differentiate polynomials, roots, and reciprocals with the power rule and find tangent lines.
Differentiate products and quotients of functions correctly using the product and quotient rules.
Differentiate composite functions by identifying inner and outer functions and applying the chain rule, alone or with other rules.
Find dy/dx for implicitly defined curves and compute tangent slopes at given points.
Compute higher-order derivatives and interpret the second derivative as acceleration or concavity.
Differentiate trigonometric functions and compositions and interpret rates in periodic models.
Differentiate exponential and logarithmic functions and explain why exponential growth has rate proportional to size.
Use the inverse-function derivative formula to compute (f^-1)' at a point and derive derivatives of inverse functions.
Construct a linearization, use it to estimate values, and judge whether the estimate is an over- or underestimate.
State the hypotheses of the Extreme Value and Mean Value Theorems and apply them to find guaranteed points.
Determine intervals of increase, decrease, and concavity from the signs of f' and f''.
Locate and classify local extrema and inflection points and justify classifications.
Formulate and solve optimization problems and justify that the solution is a global extremum.
Evaluate indeterminate limits using L'Hopital's rule after verifying the form.
Compute antiderivatives of basic functions and solve initial value problems.
Approximate definite integrals with Riemann sums and interpret them as net signed area.
Apply both parts of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to evaluate definite integrals and differentiate accumulation functions.
Use definite integrals to compute areas between curves, net change, and average values in context.
Evaluate indefinite and definite integrals using u-substitution, converting limits correctly.
Choose u and dv sensibly and evaluate integrals using integration by parts.
Decompose rational functions into partial fractions, using long division when needed, and integrate them.
